newsitem.title: FRANCE: EU says better to reform ahead of trade talks.
newsitem.headline: EU says better to reform ahead of trade talks.

text.p: A senior European Union official on Monday disputed French complaints that price-cutting farm reforms would force the EU to "pay twice" in future trade talks.
Guy Legras, director general for agriculture at the European Commission, said it was better to introduce domestic reforms first, before risking being attacked in international negotiations.

France's new Socialist-led government has criticised plans announced last week to cut dairy, cereals and beef prices from the year 2000. It says that having agreed to do this, the EU would then be forced to make further concessions to the United States in global trade negotiations due to start in 1999.

"I don't think this is a very solid argument because my experience is that it is much better to arrive at these negotiations having done your reform," Legras said, asked at a Paris news conference about the French government's criticisms.
"It does not mean you have to pay twice, it simply means that you will be in a much more solid position to negotiate with the Americans," he added.
Legras, a veteran of tough negotiations that led to the 1994 Uruguay Round pact, used similar arguments to drive through unpopular EU farm reforms in 1992 before the global trade deal was clinched.
Failing to carry out another reform this time would open the EU to attack from every angle and leave it isolated, he said.
The next round of negotiations sponsored by the World Trade Organisation is expected to force further cuts in farm spending to try to iron out unfair competition and liberalise trade.

"If we turn up in 1999 without having carried out a reform, we will be attacked on all fronts -- on border protection, on export subsidies which are the main issue for the Americans, and on our domestic support," Legras said.
He said EU negotiators would run into difficulty if they were exposed on all these fronts while lacking the "alliance of complicity" they had once enjoyed with Washington.
The United States, though bitterly opposed to Brussels during much of the last seven-year negotiation, stopped short of backing all-out free-trade since it too needed export subsidies.
Since then, Washington has suspended those subsidies and completely decoupled agricultural support from production to encourage its farmers to compete.
"They did their reform to prepare for a trade negotiation," Legras said. "With that kind of agricultural policy, they are not going to support us."

Legras was in Paris to brief French journalists on the EU reform plan, which seeks to make farmers more competitive in time for the 1999 trade talks and the bloc's eastward expansion early next century.
The Commission's Agenda 2000 plan calls for cuts of up to 30 percent in the prices guaranteed to EU farmers and a gradual shift in support towards direct payments to growers.
